name: english_02
context: An English tweet from the SemEval-2017 sentiment analysis dataset. The tweets were found by searching Twitter for popular topics of the time, such as public figures, products, places, events and political issues, and were posted between 2012 and early 2017. At least five crowd workers labelled the overall sentiment of each tweet.

versions.analysis_for_next: Version 1 was too long at 501 words, so I cut the examples to two per label and shortened every field. The fixes from version 1 stay the same. First, annotators label content as well as tone: reports of good events are positive and reports of harmful events are negative. Second, mild criticism, second-guessing, debate replies and plans are neutral. Third, event promotions and hype invitations are neutral. Negative opinions need clear hostility or sadness, and positive opinions need genuine enthusiasm.
next_examples_not_copied: Now it’s November won’t b long til Xmas music starts on VH1. Can’t wait all day everyday

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 2 broke the neutral class: neutral recall fell to 73 of 204, and macro-F1 dropped to 65.5. Calling every invitation, plan or friendly promotion positive pushed many neutral tweets to positive. Examples: 'who's up for Ant-Man', 'Don't miss the event!', 'wanna come with?', party ads. Calling every gripe or dismissive opinion negative pushed many neutral tweets to negative. Examples: sports second-guessing, political jabs, 'I'm done', 'HELL NO' at a price. Version 1 (72.0) was the better base.

I return to version 1 with narrower changes:
- Invitations, event ads, 'who's going' questions, plans and banter stay neutral.
- Positive needs the author's own clear joy, love, excitement or praise, or good news.
- Commentary or criticism aimed at teams, coaches, politicians or public figures, and political or religious argument, stay neutral unless there is open hostility or strong emotion words.
- Negative covers the author's own clear distress about their life (stuck, missed, sarcastic #not or #boring, argh) and strong contempt, plus news of violence or harm.

This keeps version 1's gains while recovering some clear personal complaints.
next_examples_not_copied: Now it’s November won’t b long til Xmas music starts on VH1. Can’t wait all day everyday

versions.analysis_for_next:
Version 3 was too neutral-heavy: 66 positive and 57 negative tweets went to neutral, and macro-F1 fell to 70.4. Version 1 (72.0) remains the best, and version 0 had more polar predictions. The best balance lies between them.

Positive tweets the model called neutral usually contain a light evaluative or warm word, even inside a promotion or plan. Examples: 'Good seats for a really good price', 'See you there!', 'best deals', ':)', 'PLEASE WIN', 'perfect', 'should be good', fun plans like Disneyland or a new apartment.

Negative tweets the model called neutral usually contain a critical judgment of a person or group. Examples: 'hypocritical', 'so bitter', 'flop', 'couldn't cope', 'not transparent', 'reject Harper', 'does nothing for me', 'Gandhi was racist'. Mild personal troubles were also missed ('haven't been able to', 'not accepting new members').

Meanwhile, neutral tweets that stayed neutral had no evaluative wording at all: logistics, bare invitations, questions, stats, headlines.

Version 4 therefore keys on evaluative language:
- Any upbeat evaluative word or emoticon, with no complaint, goes to positive. This includes promotions.
- Any critical evaluative judgment of someone or something, or a personal setback, goes to negative.
- Neutral needs no evaluation at all.

I keep the version 1 caution that 'who's going' and 'wanna come' invitations and dry score lines are neutral, since those were the neutral-to-positive errors in version 2.

Version 5 was 423 words, over the 400 limit. I trimmed one neutral example and tightened the rule; the substance is unchanged. Version 4 (72.1) lost most of neutral to negative, through sports second-guessing, political and religious debate replies, and lightly told inconveniences. It also lost neutral to positive, through event ads, plans and banter. Version 5 keeps version 4's evaluative-word approach and adds explicit neutral carve-outs for those tweet types.

Version 6 was 416 words, over the 400 limit. I removed one positive example and shortened the rule; the substance is unchanged. The base is version 4, the best so far, with narrow neutral carve-outs: tactical sports second-guessing, laughed-off hassles and court news. Mild disappointment markers such as :( and 'bummed' are explicitly negative.

Version 7 (71.6) did worse than version 6 (72.7). Making event hype without praise words neutral cost 25 extra positives to neutral. Examples: 'Christmas in September!', 'See you there!', 'omggg', 'Get your chance to win', 'Start it off with Jurassic World'. Neutral-to-negative improved only slightly (52 to 46).

I return to version 6 and make two small changes:
1. Excited exclamations about upcoming things ('omggg', 'Christmas in September!') count as positive, which reverses version 7's damage.
2. Jokes and absurd or dark humor that attack no one are neutral. This helped a few neutral-to-negative cases ('Batman put people in comas', 'scream cheater', dream jokes) without touching criticism of people.

The headline clause from version 7 is dropped, because it moved some gold-positive and gold-negative news to the wrong label. The text is trimmed to stay under 400 words.

Version 9 (72.8) is essentially version 6 again and scores the same, 72.7 to 72.8. It is the most stable and best formulation found. Every attempt to shift the neutral boundary in either direction traded errors one-for-one:
- broad neutral carve-outs (versions 3, 5 and 7) pulled positive and negative tweets into neutral;
- broad polar rules (versions 2, 4 and 8) pulled neutral tweets into the polar labels.

The remaining errors are largely ambiguous or noisy. Examples are sarcasm read as positive ('Christian Ponder would be proud', 'Thank the Gods'), dark jokes, political replies and celebrity news. Another reword is unlikely to fix them without causing new errors. For the final version I keep version 9 unchanged.
